“Hee mae mg!” (fool), my grandpa yells, his teeth clenched in frustration.

“Grandpa, what is it? Do you need your urinal bottle? Or do you want water?”

“Hee mae mg!!!”

Four years ago, I became my grandpa’s caretaker. Interpreting his needs was not easy. His face held no expression except a furrowed brow and tight lips that mouthed “Hee mae mg”. 

“Mom, how do you never get tired of his shouting?” I asked.

She showed me a photo of my grandpa and said, “From morning till night, your grandpa used to sell tofu, tirelessly riding his bicycle in the heat. I never complained because I always reminded myself of the life he used to have.”

Looking at his pictures, I began to see the person he used to be. One struck me: he was spinning, and swinging his arms in the air. Now, he was confined to his bed, watching the world pass him by. I quickly realized then that he must have been scared of losing touch with life itself. Perhaps his screams were a mask for that fear. Feeling guilty for misunderstanding him, I decided to change the way I communicate with him.

Sensing the impact photos had on me, I wondered if they might have the same effect on him. I crafted my own album to share with him. 

Recognizing how isolated he must have felt, I began collecting the moments we missed together. I stood beside him and showed him pictures of my family’s Osaka trip, where we rode a Harry Potter-themed rollercoaster—my mom and I with our eyes shut, and my brother and dad’s eyes sparkling with excitement, their mouths wide open. I wanted to share these exciting and memorable feelings with him, to make him feel included in our family. When my grandpa calmed down, I felt relieved. We created our own silent language—it may not have been like others, but it was enough for my grandpa and me to understand.

Reflecting on our way of communicating, I realized that I could use the language I created to address the communication barriers that Laotians face due to the lack of access to literacy resources that limits their expression of ideas. Since Lao is a language built on compound words, I had the idea of putting a photo on top of each word. That way, Laotians could associate the composition of each word with an image, developing their literacy skills. Furthermore, inspired by the lessons learned through my grandpa’s stories, I created a visual storybook where Laotians can read with their family and share meaningful moments together. With these combined visions, I created LittleStories, an early-education reading tool.

While I was at my cousin’s house, I met five-year-old Somphone and decided to test the efficiency of my books. From reading Emma’s Passion to The Hardworking Turtle, I taught her how to read, write, and pronounce words in Lao. Every time she differentiates the word pattern between mae (bus) and maae (mom), I am reminded of creating language to communicate with my grandpa, using pictures to express what words could not. Watching Somphone learn new words and seeing my grandpa’s warm look, I’m amazed by how communication stretches beyond words. 

The room next door no longer echoes “Hee mae mg.” It's empty now, filled only with memories. Yet, I still visit to talk to my grandpa, whose presence is captured both in the frames that decorate our shelves and the photo albums resting on our tables. From the start to the end, our communication was never “normal,” but we still managed to understand one another across generations and cultural differences. In college, I hope to keep discovering new forms of communication—verbal or otherwise.

At three a.m., I found myself once again surrounded by the wreckage of my broken promises. The dim glow of my phone revealed a familiar scene of defeat: a sea of crumpled chip bags, grease-stained pizza boxes, and donut crumbs. I swore I wouldn’t binge again, yet each time, the urge would drown my determination like a wave swallowing a storm. My life unfolded like The Truman Show; I watched myself follow a path of scripted choices I couldn’t escape. Why did I keep repeating the same cycle? Was it comfort, or was I avoiding something worse? If I was serious about change, I knew I had to look inward, questioning the comfort I found in self-sabotage and confronting the truths I had avoided for so long.

The summer after my sophomore year, I immersed myself in studying human biology. YouTube videos on eating behaviors became nightly rituals, starting with Professor Andrew Huberman’s series on how dopamine pathways control reward-seeking behaviors. I kept rewinding the episode, taking notes as he explained intricate concepts foreign to me. Day after day, “just one more video” turned into late-night research dives, my cravings for junk food replaced with a hunger for knowledge. Eventually, the videos weren’t enough—I began poring over the precision of scientific literature.

Gaining new vocabulary like 'endorphins' and 'serotonin' helped me see my cravings differently—suddenly they became patterns I could understand, not impulses I had to obey. Each binge brought a numbing endorphin high, but as serotonin levels dipped, relief soon turned to anxiety. As my understanding of human health grew, I started to approach each urge with curiosity rather than judgement. When I felt the familiar pull toward the fridge late at night, I practiced deep breathing to calm my racing thoughts. I began journaling each time I overcame an urge to record these small victories. Slowly, these actions built a foundation of resilience, transforming my relationship with food and allowing me to regain control. Overcoming my own battle awakened a new hunger to use my experience to support others with their own limitations. This time, the urge pushing me forward was constructive and aligned with my values. My internship at the Houston Rheumatology Center took on new meaning as I realized my struggles had equipped me to offer genuine understanding and support to patients like never before.

One evening, an elderly patient approached me, gripping her walker tightly as she watched younger patients enjoying physical therapy together. “I just can’t keep up like I used to,” she sighed. I could see how the stiffness in her joints left her feeling trapped in her own body. My struggle with binging taught me that discomfort—physical or mental—could make small tasks feel impossible. I wanted to help her regain a sense of control by creating exercises that respected her limits yet rekindled the joy of movement. That night, I researched physical therapy, looking for evidence-based strategies tailored for patients with limited mobility. Inspired, I used Canva to design simple brochures with simple instructions and colorful graphics, then printed them in bulk. I offered them to patients who expressed interest or mentioned pain when trying standard exercises, hoping the knowledge within those pages could help them reclaim their independence. The overwhelming support from patients inspired me to organize community events, where I led elderly patients through these accessible exercises. Through their feedback, I saw how scientific knowledge, when paired with empathy, could uplift an entire community by giving them the tools to regain control over their lives.


Three a.m. used to be a time of broken promises and uncontrollable cravings. Now, I’m kept up by a different desire - one to bring comfort, resources, and empowerment to those who are in need. As I walk this path, I hope to offer others the empathy and support I once needed, bringing my hard-earned understanding to those facing their own battles.

The year is 1983. My father’s family flees Sri Lanka at the peak of Black July. Their home was vandalized by Sinhalese mobs. In the north, his uncle rides home with mangoes tied to the spokes of his bicycle. He is stopped in the street by two men, who ask if he is Sinhalese or Tamil. He answers Tamil. They shoot him. A few miles away, my mother crouches under a bus seat as shells rain down outside the vehicle. She survives. Her parents put her on a train back to Colombo, praying she will escape the hotspot of political violence. 

2001. My father and mother, newly married, move into their first apartment in America. The shoebox-sized studio has barely enough space to move, but it is home. They eat cold bagels and cereal and toaster strudel. True American delicacies. 

2014. My first trip to Sri Lanka. I am seven years old. Moisture weighs down the air wherever we go. The floors look dirty to me, not like American floors. Bumps the size of small moons pepper my arms and legs, gifts from the mosquitoes. Selfishly, I rage at my parents for bringing me to this place. We go to the temple in the morning, drink tea, and hide from the afternoon heat in my grandmother’s foyer. We wait and wait and wait. Neighbors come and go through the open door. Palm trees share hushed whispers in the ocean’s breeze. The light flickers, on, off, on, off. I wonder what we are waiting for.

2020. I attend my first protest for Black Lives Matter. My sister and I proudly hoist our sign; a big, dark fist emblazoned on Amazon cardboard. Five minutes into the march it begins to rain. Behind my hood and mask, my unsmiling face is barely visible. I clear my throat and join in the chants. No justice! No peace! The only response is the rain beginning to fall harder, and cars honking as they go by. In support or in jest, I don’t know. Something inside tells me to yell louder, stand up taller. It says yes, here. This is what I’m meant to do.

2022. My last trip to Sri Lanka. I am fifteen years old. My grandparents’ driver waits in line for three nights to get petrol and cooking gas for the house. On the streets, others do the same. They wait and wait and wait, falling asleep in their rickshaws. Fuel is quickly running out. Protestors camp outside Parliament in masses. They call it aragalaya, struggle, and wave flags. Like the lion on them, they roar—Go home, Gota! The government passes a national curfew, then they begin using tear gas and water cannons. The protestors become more inflamed. They are sick of waiting. They unleash fire on the prime minister’s house and storm the presidential palace. They jump in Gota’s pool, sleep in his bed, and dance exuberantly to trumpets in the hallways. The president flees to the Maldives. Smoke spirals in the sky. I forget about the mosquitoes.

Sri Lanka has shown me waiting in many forms. Irritated by the stupor of my childhood visits, I looked down on the country from the comfort of my American standards. After my first protest, I didn’t know it’d mark the start, not the end, of my journey to speak out. What I did understand was that fighting for justice isn’t always loud or immediate. It’s built over time, and waiting is simply preparation for action. My family’s sacrifices in escaping persecution and the protests manifesting in Sri Lanka forty years later show true advocacy is perseverance. It’s a never-ending cycle, from injustice, to progress, and back again. These acts of defiance, however loud or quiet, are important.

We reinforced each other’s beliefs without challenging them, and I settled in, delighted at having found my comfort zone.
During a class debate on the government’s renewable energy programs one morning, I supported a complete shift to green energy. A classmate countered me, raising concerns about infrastructure costs and the threat of unemployment. Instead of listening and responding, I felt challenged and reacted. We both argued for the last word, refusing common ground.
 
Reflecting on this, I realized I’d built my own echo chamber with my small coterie, a space where my opinions were validated without room for growth. I decided to expand my horizons by seeking people with divergent experiences and perspectives.
 
Going to the movies with my different-abled friend, Rohan, made me realize how uncomfortable and inconvenient the place I enjoyed was for him due to its lack of inclusive infrastructure. I thought mastering yoga would make me a superhero; it turns out I was right. As I take a step onto the mat, a sense of calm prevails as all the worries in the world slowly dissipate. The familiar feel of the spongy cushion and the stimulating aroma of the rubber scent ground me. As I begin my routine with the Urdhva Hastasana—the upward salute pose—I feel every part of my body come alive and work together in harmony. My arms stretch with agility, complementing the flexibility of my spine. Having moved between three countries during high school, my identity often felt lost and I was unsure of my roots. Yoga has provided the grounding I needed, being a constant in my life that never made me forget who I was.

From the very first time I caught sight of my mom doing yoga as a five-year-old, I was obsessed with mimicking her every movement with my chubby hands and little stout feet. Despite falling over and over as I attempted the child pose, I was resilient in my approach. I just wanted to do it as eloquently as my mom did. Just as I learned to hold the pose, eventually, I learned to hold my ground during challenges. My diagnosis of Scoliosis my freshman year didn’t prevent me from undertaking 4 varsity sports, nor did my family’s immigration issues deter me from building an inspiring science community, AspireSTEM, in every place I called home.

The beauty of every pose, complexity of every stretch, and dynamics of the breathing technique always filled my head with endless thoughts. “Ma, what is the science behind the breathing technique?” “Ma, how does the pose get its name?” Each question led me to a new path. That childhood fascination stayed through all of my adolescence, slowly blossoming my curiosity into an insatiable desire to learn, not just about yoga but the world around me. From Aristotle's philosophies to Mendelian genetics, I spared nothing that I got my hands on.

Yoga fueled my unparalleled desire to try new poses as I mastered the basics. Eagle pose, frog pose, cow pose—you name it. I still remember vividly the day I finally mastered the child pose, or I felt like I did, swelling with pride as if I had conquered the world. That feeling mirrored the pride I felt growing my first micro-green at age ten or when I rooted for Mohawk, Africa’s oldest lion, to survive another day in the documentaries I obsessively watched. 

Ending my yoga session with Savasana, joy and sadness bubble within me. I am devastated that the ritual has to come to a closing but grateful that I will be able to do it all over again tomorrow. Importantly, I gain mental clarity on my journey in yoga, and life. Yoga has given rise to an unbreakable bond with my mom who inspires me every day, and I am confident I will find fellow yoga enthusiasts to connect and forge bonds with, sharing stories, laughter, sweat, and even tears.

The balance I find on the mat reflects my pursuit of balance in other aspects of my life, from dance rehearsals and basketball practices to computational biology research. As I take a step closer to adulthood, I carry with me lessons yoga has taught me. I will always be the googly-eyed toddler who can’t wait to do yoga, and the mat will always remain my superhero training ground to connect with myself when life gets challenging. As I step off the mat, my session doesn’t end here; rather I see a cape ready to be put on for my next adventure, finding passions both on and off the mat. I will pursue each experience with purpose and enthusiasm, honoring the beauty of the journey itself. With each deep breath, I remind myself life, like yoga, is not perfect but infused with lifelong memories.

“I’m more of a son than my brothers are anyway,” chimed the voice in my head. I fumbled with a red strip of fabric pilfered from Ayah’s closet dangling around my neck like a self-bestowed medallion. The phone on the desk played a video: How to Tie a Tie (EASY). 

I pinched the wide end of the tie and crossed it over the narrow one, forming an X. This––the voice declared––was justice!

A batik-patterned shawl sulked at the desk’s edge, protesting at being forsaken. I ignored it, of course. Why must I, a grown 13 year old, listen to a deceptively beautiful leash? 

“Wear this to the wedding,” Ibu* said earlier, shoving the shawl into my hands alongside an overly-embellished dress that made an impossible feat of walking without tripping. I stopped myself from asking her “why?”––a word she surely is sick of hearing by now since I abused it at every opportunity: why are speed bumps called “sleeping officers”? Were police killed as ritual sacrifice and buried there? Why are many bowls decorated with roosters? To affirm the superiority of the Rooster zodiac? Why can’t I wear what my brothers wore––loose, minimal, while free of scrutiny? Some questions she answered briskly, others vaguely, oftentimes with the dreaded “that’s just how it is.”

Being the only daughter meant noticing double standards early, how I wasn’t allowed to do certain things my brothers could, and neither could Ibu, who compliantly stopped leading prayers to let my brothers, much younger and less experienced, lead, who dismissed feminism as a “western-import,” who often answered my questions with “that’s just how it is,” who did not question at all. 

I looped the wide end under the narrow one. Despite being a daughter, I knew I could become the ideal son. When Ibu complained that none of her sons were doing their jobs by watching soccer with Ayah, I stepped in, sitting with other men on benches to shout “GOAAAL!” to all the wrong times.

I pulled the tie through the loop and tugged down. Engaging and competing in martial arts became proof of my value. In Taekwondo practice, when a boy hits hard, I’d try hitting harder. 

I slipped the wide end underneath, through the opening. At school, I insisted on wearing trousers over skirts, negotiating with teachers to tweak the uniform policy to accord all students greater freedom to choose. 

Knot cinched, the tie was a rather meaningless defiance. But it was something others would not allow and that made it worthwhile. 

-

In the car, I sat next to Ibu. She glanced at me. “Why are you wearing that?! It looks ridiculous. I gave you the shawl.” 

I couldn’t hold in the W-word anymore. “Why do I have to wear that?”

“Dress code.”

“So, I have to wear it while they–,” I pointed to my brothers, ”–don’t?”

“What? No! Everyone’s using it. Look, Armand’s already wearing his.”

I twisted from my seat to look at my brother. To my horror, there he was. Sitting. Shawl over his shoulders. 

Guilt settled as realisation dawned: I had fancied myself superior for being a skeptic and based my self-worth on my ability to be the “better son,” to surpass others’ expectations, real or perceived. In my insecurity, I became quick to make assumptions and shut my ears, creating a falsified image of others, of my own mother. As a successful woman and engineer, she had battled expectations herself and won––victories I foolishly dismissed. I questioned everything, yet I failed to question myself and my facile judgments. 

Beyond learning how to ask for clarifications, I began to appreciate the nuance in others’ beliefs and experiences: I’ve come to value debates with family and friends, seeked their life stories, and go opinion-hunting––even if we’ve disagreed.

Nearing the venue, I pulled out the shawl and confessed to Ibu: “I’m not sure how to wear this.”

“Here. I’ll help.”

*Ibu = Mother
*Ayah = Father

A batik-patterned shawl sulked at the desk’s edge, protesting at being forsaken. I ignored it, of course. Why must I, a grown 13 year old, listen to a deceptively beautiful leash?

“Wear this to the wedding,” Ibu said earlier, shoving the shawl into my hands alongside an overly-embellished dress that made an impossible feat of walking without tripping. I stopped myself from asking her “why?”––a word she surely is sick of hearing by now since I abused it at every opportunity: why are speed bumps called “sleeping officers”? Were police killed as ritual sacrifice and buried there? Why are many bowls decorated with roosters? To affirm the superiority of the Rooster zodiac? Why can’t I wear what my brothers wore––loose, minimal, while free of scrutiny? Some questions she answered briskly, others vaguely, oftentimes with the dreaded “that’s just how it is.”

Being the only daughter meant noticing double standards early, how I wasn’t allowed to do certain things my brothers could, and neither could Ibu, who compliantly stopped leading prayers to let my brothers, much younger and less experienced, lead, who dismissed feminism as a “western-import,” who often answered my questions with “that’s just how it is,” who did not question at all.

I looped the wide end under the narrow one. Despite being a daughter, I knew I could become the ideal son. When Ibu complained that none of her sons were doing their jobs by watching soccer with Ayah, I stepped in, sitting with other men on benches to shout “GOAAAL!” to all the wrong times.

I pulled the tie through the loop and tugged down. Engaging and competing in martial arts became proof of my value. In Taekwondo practice, when a boy hits hard, I’d try hitting harder.

I slipped the wide end underneath, through the opening. At school, I insisted on wearing trousers over skirts, negotiating with teachers to tweak the uniform policy to accord all students greater freedom to choose.

Knot cinched, the tie was a rather meaningless defiance. But it was something others would not allow and that made it worthwhile.

In the car, I sat next to Ibu. She glanced at me. “Why are you wearing that?! It looks ridiculous. I gave you the shawl.”

I couldn’t hold in the W-word anymore. “Why do I have to wear that?”

“Dress code.”

“So, I have to wear it while they–,” I pointed to my brothers, ”–don’t?”

“What? No! Everyone’s using it. Look, Armand’s already wearing his.”

I twisted from my seat to look at my brother. To my horror, there he was. Sitting. Shawl over his shoulders.

Guilt settled as realisation dawned: I had fancied myself superior for being a skeptic and based my self-worth on my ability to be the “better son,” to surpass others’ expectations, real or perceived. In my insecurity, I became quick to make assumptions and shut my ears, creating a falsified image of others, of my own mother. As a successful woman and engineer, she had battled expectations herself and won––victories I foolishly dismissed. I questioned everything, yet I failed to question myself and my facile judgments.

Beyond learning how to ask for clarifications, I began to appreciate the nuance in others’ beliefs and experiences: I’ve come to value debates with family and friends, seeked their life stories, and go opinion-hunting––even if we’ve disagreed.

Nearing the venue, I pulled out the shawl and confessed to Ibu: “I’m not sure how to wear this.”

“Here. I’ll help.”

His sharp words and erratic behavior frustrated me. My fury boiled over when my brother smashed my computer in yet another argument. I snapped words meant to stab. 

“You always complain about Dad being the problem, but the role he plays in your life – you play that exact role in mine.” My brother, who was never at a loss for words, stood silent. 

I won! I finally silenced him. 

But the triumph was hollow, dissipating almost as quickly as it came. In the aftermath, I was left with unsettling questions that refused to be ignored. Where was the issue?

One evening, after yet another argument with our mother, he stormed into my room. “I hate myself for how I act. All I want is to get along with everyone.” His vulnerability caught me off guard. He expressed insecurities and pain he had never expressed before. For the first time, I saw beyond his anger and saw someone struggling with his loneliness. That moment cracked the shades of resentment. I began to see how my resentment had blinded me –- not only to his humanity but also to the capacity of my own. 

“Want to watch a movie?” he’d ask, and I’d always reply, “Not now, I’m busy.” I couldn’t understand why he couldn’t just watch the movie on his own. I was only protecting my time, but now I realized how often I had dismissed his attempts to connect. Our conflicts weren’t about winning or losing; they were cries for understanding, both his and mine. Compassion began to seep into spaces once filled with anger. I discovered the power of empathy — not as an obligation but as a choice that could set me free. 

“Want to watch a movie?” I asked. He just smiled and said a big, “Sure!” I began to see that connection was such a simple human need but meeting that need was transformative. The simple act of reaching out first began to change our relationship. I couldn’t meet him where he was at all times, but fury was replaced with understanding and bonding. 

I sat down and came to reflect on that change, wondering how often others might feel the same loneliness my brother did but had no place to belong to. I thought about what I could implement in my community in the roles I was in. When I founded the Korean American Student Association at my highschool, my goal was to connect people of shared heritage. But as I grew, so did my vision. People from different backgrounds often wanted to join but hesitated, unsure if they could truly belong. I saw this as a chance to create a space they would also feel welcome in. 

What is the best way to bond different people? A good challenge. That’s how the Spicy Buldak Challenge was born. I thought about how laughter and the shared struggle to eat something impossibly spicy could bring people together. Coordinating the event wasn’t easy, but I believed it was worth it. Thirteen participants braved the spicy Buldak challenge, cheered on by an audience of over thirty students from diverse backgrounds. Students came up to me to express how much fun they’d had and signed up to join the club. The event was a success! The club grew to become a safe space where students could feel connected where they might feel lost in the mass.

His sharp words and erratic behavior frustrated me. My fury boiled over when my brother smashed my computer in yet another argument. I snapped words meant to stab. 

“You always complain about Dad being the problem, but the role he plays in your life – you play that exact role in mine.” My brother, who was never at a loss for words, stood silent. 

I won! I finally silenced him. 

But the triumph was hollow, dissipating almost as quickly as it came. In the aftermath, I was left with unsettling questions that refused to be ignored. Where was the issue?

He expressed insecurities and pain he had never expressed before. For the first time, I saw beyond his anger and saw someone struggling with his loneliness. That moment cracked the shades of resentment. I began to see how my resentment had blinded me –- not only to his humanity but also to the capacity of my own. 

“Want to watch a movie?” he’d ask, and I’d always reply, “Not now, I’m busy.” I couldn’t understand why he couldn’t just watch the movie on his own. I was only protecting my time, but now I realized how often I had dismissed his attempts to connect. Our conflicts weren’t about winning or losing; they were cries for understanding, both his and mine. Compassion began to seep into spaces once filled with anger. I discovered the power of empathy — not as an obligation but as a choice that could set me free. 

“Want to watch a movie?” I asked. He just smiled and said a big, “Sure!” I began to see that connection was such a simple human need but meeting that need was transformative. The simple act of reaching out first began to change our relationship. I couldn’t meet him where he was at all times, but fury was replaced with understanding and bonding. 

I sat down and came to reflect on that change, wondering how often others might feel the same loneliness my brother did but had no place to belong to. I thought about what I could implement in my community in the roles I was in. When I founded the Korean American Student Association at my high school, my goal was to connect people of shared heritage. But as I grew, so did my vision. The club grew to become a safe space where students could feel connected where they might feel lost in the mass.
